title: Netflix's Reed Hastings Provides Example #534,215 of Why Free Market And Education Are A Bad Match
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene uses Netflix founder Reed Hastings' reversal on ad-supported streaming to satirise where market-driven school choice leads. His argument is that markets sort customers into tiers, so choice means only the choice you can afford. He imagines lower-tier voucher students receiving ad-supported instruction while wealthier families buy an ad-free version. The piece applies the internet maxim that if you are not paying you are the product to children as a captive audience. He points to Channel One as precedent and warns that privatised schooling will revive the ad-supported model once marketers meet marketers. It is short policy commentary in his usual sardonic register, closest in the archive to his school-policy and charter commentary.
points: Tiered markets mean school choice is really choice you can afford, so lower-income students end up in the cheaper tier.
The article extends the streaming ad-tier model to schooling, imagining sponsored classes for voucher students.
Greene argues that student attention and data are an untapped revenue stream that only parent and educator objections currently protect.
Channel One is offered as evidence that ad-supported schooling has been tried and would return once it can.
quotes: In the world of market driven school choice, there will, of course, be tiers. There is no market that doesn't do this, because one of the things the free market is good for is sorting customers and vendors into tiers.
You can buy a Lexus or a used Yugo. Tiy can shop on Rodeo Drive or at Walmart. In short, free market choice really means that you can have all the choice you can afford.

Folks at pricey private school get, well, school. Meanwhile, on the lower tiers where students have to depend on meager voucher amounts and shrinking taxpayer subsidies, students get to attend "The Pepsi Corp Algebra II Class, brought to you today by Diet Pepsi.

It's one of the unstated economic pressures to privatize. We now all know one lesson of the internet--if you are not paying for the service, then you are actually the product. If you aren't buying, then you're the one being sold.

This is not even a new idea--remember the whole idea of Channel One was "We'll show your students some news and you'll let us show them some marketing." Don't imagine for a moment that privatized school won't bring that "ad-supported model" back the first minute they think they can.
